Property rights have always contained four elements:

  1. the right to use

  2. the right to exclude others from use

  3. the right to transfer ownership

  4. the right to modify or destroy

As we can plainly see, rights # 3 and 4 are not met.

Software is not property. People need to know this. Thank you GM for inadvertently publicizing this.

With cars this is not a big deal. It's always been that way with proprietary technology. All auto manufacturers do the same to protect their licenses and technology. Imagine the shitstorm if the CPU goodies were leaked and someone found a way to control GM vehicles. Their ability to update firmware is an important part of safety and security.

An attorney from the Electronic Frontier Foundation also testified at the hearing, telling the Copyright Office that restricting access to onboard computers in vehicles drives up costs, hurts competition, and stifles innovation. It also prevents third party researchers from conducting independent safety and security research without becoming lawbreakers.

This is BS. It's up to the auto manufacturer to make sure the vehicle in it's entirety is safe. They get the backlash if things screw up. That's a far better deterrent against shoddy practices than a safety panel could ever be.

There are plenty of times the minimum wage has been raised substantially in a localized area giving plenty of data to draw educated predictions from, but the thing that really got to me was suggesting that it will be the highest minimum wage among the richest countries in the world. Good working conditions and a less corrupt government completely negate the need for a minimum wage. There actually is no minimum wage in countries like Norway, Denmark and Sweden. I agree setting the minimum wage to $75, which would effectively put somebody in the top 5% of income earners would not be wise, however that has really nothing to do with anything here. $15/hour in still puts somebody well into the lower half of earners country wide. In LA it's going to be something rather less than that. It's not going to be much more than a livable wage.

Consider that when we set the minimum wage below the amount needed for an individual to live a satisfactory life that individual is going to end up ultimately on various government social programs be it SNAP, welfare, or what not. It's been estimated that the cost for this to taxpayers for WalMart -alone- is more than $6 billion a year. When you think of things like welfare your tax dollars are effectively going into the pockets of companies like WalMart. They don't pay a livable wage, so the government gets the taxpayers to subsidize their wages.

I think the natural retort here should be something like, "Well. People shouldn't be living off min wage jobs. It's a springboard to better things." You can check out wage data in the US here. Suffice to say it's not a springboard. There just aren't many well paying jobs in the US. The median hourly wage in the US is currently about $17 - in other words 50% of jobs pay that or even less. As intelligent automation takes off that number is likely to see substantial declines so something is going to have to change.
Have you considered the possibility that people whom you've never met, hundreds of miles away from you, perhaps have a better idea of what to charge for their time than you do?

The employment system in the US works almost entirely off coercion. People work not because they feel their time is being fairly valued, but because if they don't - they starve. One of the major impetuses here was protests across the country of tens of thousands of workers seeking a livable wage.

In a country where work was not coercive then I'd agree that there'd be no need for a minimum wage. Or in a country where workers were allowed to engage in collective bargaining to come to mutually beneficial rates there's also no need for a minimum wage. But work in the US is coercive and workers are legally prohibited from organizing or their capacity in organization is hamstrung depending on the state. In this situation you need a minimum wage or you're going to inevitably face a tragedy of the commons.
